title: The Industrial Relations and OSH Codes: what BMS objects to
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The anti-worker provisions that BMS wants changed.
body:
BMS welcomed the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security. On the **Industrial Relations Code** and the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code**, its statements in 2026 spoke of **anti-worker provisions** that it wants corrected. This post explains the position as BMS has stated it, sets out what the two Codes actually provide, and shows what the process from here looks like.

## Where the Codes stand

The four Labour Codes were brought into force on 21 November 2025. Together they merge 29 earlier central labour laws, many dating from the 1930s to the 1950s. The Government's press release said they would bring written appointment letters for all workers, gratuity for fixed-term employees after one year instead of five, a national floor wage, legal recognition of gig and platform workers for the first time, and wider social security. It put social security coverage at about 19 per cent of the workforce in 2015 and more than 64 per cent in 2025. The Prime Minister described the reform as among the most progressive since Independence, and industry bodies called it a historic milestone. Some trade unions, in contrast, have called the Codes a death knell for job security.

## What BMS has said

BMS's position is mixed, and it is important to describe it accurately. At its all-India working committee meeting in Ranchi on 26 to 28 July 2026, BMS endorsed the Wage Code and the Social Security Code as steps in workers' interest. It recorded objections on **13 points** in the Industrial Relations Code, concerning among other things the definitions of "industry", "wages" and "worker", the recognition of negotiating unions and provisions on annual returns, and argued that the present text could weaken trade unions and collective bargaining. On the OSH Code it objected to **15 provisions**, including the definitions of "factory" and "work activity" and rules on safety and health standards, and said there can be no compromise on workers' safety. The reported stance is that BMS is not opposing the Codes outright. It wants amendments to protect workers' rights, job security and dignity, and uniform implementation across sectors. BMS's objections to two of the four Codes were reported as early as February 2025.

On 17 August 2026 BMS repeated, in its nationwide demonstrations, that the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code contain many anti-worker provisions and asked the Government to hold talks with the central trade unions and bring in amendments. On 1 September, BMS reported that the Labour Minister gave an assurance of early amendments, though its note gave no details of which provisions or when.

## What the two Codes provide on the commonly debated points

The following points are drawn from published summaries of the Codes. Readers should note that BMS's own 13-point and 15-point lists are set out in its memoranda, and the points below are not a substitute for them. Some are issues that unions of all kinds have raised.

**Industrial Relations Code**
- **Thresholds.** Establishments with 300 or more workers must have certified standing orders, and need the appropriate Government's permission before layoff, retrenchment or closure. The earlier figure was 100. The Central or State Government may raise the 300 threshold by notification and can exempt new establishments from provisions in the public interest.
- **Strikes.** A strike or lockout requires 60 days' notice and a 14-day waiting period after notice is given, and mass casual leave by half the workers on a day is treated as a strike.
- **Negotiating union.** Where there are several registered unions, a union backed by at least 51 per cent of workers is the sole negotiating union. If none reaches that level, a negotiating council can be formed from unions with at least 20 per cent verified support.
- **Fixed-term employment.** Fixed-term workers receive proportionate benefits and are eligible for gratuity after one year of service. Unions ask for safeguards against replacing permanent staff with fixed-term workers.
- **Reskilling fund.** For each retrenched worker, the employer must deposit 15 days' wages, and the amount is to reach the worker within 45 days.
- **Grievance committee.** Establishments with 20 or more workers need a grievance committee of ten members with equal representation.

**OSH Code**
- **Contract labour.** Contract workers may be engaged in core activities in certain cases, such as where the work is normally outsourced, does not need full-time involvement, or arises from a temporary increase in workload.
- **Registration.** Establishments with ten or more employees need a single electronic registration.
- **Other provisions.** Appointment letters are mandatory, overtime needs the worker's consent and is paid at twice the normal rate, a National OSH Board is created, and safety committees are required in establishments with over 500 workers.

## Why these points matter to workers

A higher threshold for permission means that an establishment with, say, 200 workers can lay off or close without prior approval. A longer notice period for strikes narrows a union's room to act. Recognition rules decide who may bargain for the workers. Contract-labour rules decide whether a worker doing core work gets the same status as a permanent one. Definitions of "factory" and "worker" decide who falls within the law's protection at all. Even small changes of wording can therefore move large numbers of workers in or out of coverage, which is why BMS's objections concentrate on definitions.

## How the process works

The Codes allow **State Governments** to adopt higher thresholds or add protections through rules, and the appropriate Government is empowered to adjust some thresholds by notification. Hence, after the Centre's action, the next battleground is each State's rules, where unions can ask for the best terms. Amendments to the Codes themselves require Parliament. Employers must comply with both existing laws and the new Codes until the transition is complete, according to one law-firm summary.

## Where to read the actual text

BMS's specific list is set out in its memoranda on the BMS website. We encourage readers to look at those and to read the Codes themselves on India Code and the Ministry of Labour website, and not rely on this summary. PRS Legislative Research publishes neutral summaries.

## For karyakartas

- Read the Code and the draft rules of your State and compare them with your members' needs.
- Note how many workers your own establishment employs, since several rights turn on the number.
- Write to the State labour department with specific amendments, and keep a copy.
- Report cases where appointment letters, floor wages or the written terms of fixed-term workers are not being followed.
